Introduce TypeDef, and support for __getattr__ and __setattr__

This is a breakthrough.

This PR introduces `TypeDef`, which makes it possible to define a static-type alias of another type. The big news is that you can attach custom (blue) `__getattr__` and `__setattr__` to the typedef, and these calls will be redshifted away.

It needs more polishing: currently we support implicit conversion from and to the TypeDef, but only because we don't support enough of the language to have a better way. Ideally, I would like a `cast[T]` function.

subject: Merge pull request #48 from spylang/refactor-FQN
message:
Merge pull request #48 from spylang/refactor-FQN

Introduce the distinction between QN and FQN

Split the old FQN into two different types:

A Qualified Name (QN) locates a function or class inside the source code, e.g. test::foo.
A Fully Qualified Name (FQN) can exists only in the context of a specific VM and must be unique. You can have multiple FQNs mapping to the same QN, e.g. in case of closures: test::foo#0, test::foo#1, etc.

Among the other things, this makes much easier to write OPERATORS at interp level, because now we can just return an interp-level closure with a QN, and the doppler will take care of turning it into an FQN when appropriate.

message:
Merge pull request #57 from spylang/call-method

Introduce CALL_METHOD as a 1st-class operator

This is a bit of a departure from the standard Python semantics but I believe it makes many common patterns easier to write (and possibly more efficient).

Normally, the pattern a.b(...) is parsed as a Call(GetAttr(), ...), but with this PR we special-case this syntax and we produce CallMethod(...). Objects can then implement their own operator to implement it.

This will be useful for example to implement a Javascript FFI, because JS doesn't have the concept of bound methods.

In the future, we will probably implement a default CALL_METHOD which is implemented in terms of getattr+call.

subject: Merge pull request #59 from spylang/universal-equality
message:
Merge pull request #59 from spylang/universal-equality

This PR introduces the concepts of "storage categories" and "universal equality".
As a result, we are able to fix one of the 3 "FIXME" which were introduced by PR #58.

Storage category is used to distinguish between "value types" and "reference types":

  - value types: (e.g. i32, f64, but also str and eventually user-defined structs) don't have the concept of identity and the operator `is` is forbidden on them (well, it will be, since `is` has not been implemented yet).
    This is a departure from Python semantics, but arguably using `is` on primitive types is almost always wrong and leads to subtle bugs (such as `if x is 'hello'` or `if x is 42`, which might or might not work depending on the phase of the moon).

  - reference types: objects have an identity and `is` can be used. Moreover, by default `==` is implemented in term of `is` for them.

On top of that, we introduce the concept of "universal equality". This tries to find a balance between what you would expect in a statically typed language and the usual Python semantics.
The TL;DR version is:

- equality (or "strict equality") is permitted only if types are related. E.g. doing `42 == "hello"` is a TypeError. This is what you would expect by a statically typed language.

- universal equality is more relaxed: it allows to compare objects of different types, and e.g. `42` is not equal to `"hello"`. This is closer to Python semantics and it's useful when writing generic code, e.g. if the objects are used as keys for a cache, or similar.

The trick is that when types are statically known, the token `==` corresponds to strict equality. Thus, the following code raises TypeError (either at runtime or compile time, depending on lazy vs eager errors):
```
a: i32 = 42
b: str = "hello"
print(a == b)
```

But if the types are `dynamic`, then we switch to universal equality. So the following prints `False`:
```
a: dynamic = 42
b: dynamic = "hello"
print(a == b)
```

Eventually, it will be possible to explicitly call universal vs strict equality by calling `operator.eq` and `operator.universal_eq`, but these has not been implemented yet.

Armed with this, we can kill this horrible hack:
https://github.com/spylang/spy/blob/c58a82f1881432f72e00f89c5bd74423fb9fde46/spy/vm/vm.py#L293-L301 

Now `bluecache.looukup` uses universal equality to compare arguments.

subject: Introduce W_OpImpl.with_values (#66)
message:
Introduce W_OpImpl.with_values (#66)

This is a big refactoring in how OPERATORS, the vm and the typechecker
play all together.

Old-style operators receive argument types, and return a function to be
called on those arguments.

New-style operators receive abstract "Values", which also have a type
but also represent a placeholder for the actual values which will be
computed at runtime. They can decide to pass these Values in any order
to the opimpl, but also discard them, or in the future to add type
conversions, etc.

Contrarily to old-style, it's the job of new-style operators to raise a
proper `SPyTypeError`.
This ensures that you get high-quality errors even at runtime (e.g. by
calling `vm.getitem` or so).

Compile-time type errors are no longer explicitly raised by the
typechecker, but naturally come from redshifting blue OPERATOR calls.

So far, only `op.GETITEM` is new-style, more will follow

subject: Add support for low-level unsafe allocation and manipulation of structs (#82)
message:
Add support for low-level unsafe allocation and manipulation of structs (#82)

Support for the `class` statements in:
  - parser
  - ScopeAnalizer (but there is a bug, see later)
  - modgen
  - astframe

`struct` is a special keyword that can be used as a base class to
declare structs, like this:
```
class Point(struct):
    x: i32
    y: i32
```

For now, it is possible to do only low-level manipulation of structs,
using the `unsafe` module. Attribute access is mapped to special
`getfield` and `setfield` builtin functions which are then special-cased
by the C backend to generate good-looking C code.

Misc changes:
  - super hackish support for "constant" `W_Value`: see below.
- `vm.call_generic`, which is just a shortcut but makes code a bit
easier to read
  - add a pytest `--dump-c` option


The PR is already big and complex enough that it's a good idea to merge
it soon, but it introduces some workarounds/hackish solutions to
problems that will be solved by follow-up PRs.

In particular:
- scope of the `class` statement: this is semi-broken because inner
declarations are evaluated inside the module scope, instead of creating
its own
- "constant" `W_Value`: currently it's very and we use a special value
`999` to distinguish them from non-constant values, but it's clearly a
hack
- FQN of types: we currently don't assign an FQN to types, but in order
to do so we probably need to tweak a bit how (F)QNs are structured: we
probably want to introduce more nested namespaces

subject: Kill QN, and just use FQN everywhere (#91)
message:
Kill QN, and just use FQN everywhere (#91)

This is the last step of a multi-PRs journey to refactor FQNs.

The idea of having a separate notion of QN (which is more "abstract")
and FQN (which can only be assigned by the VM) is nice in theory but
proved to cause a lot of hassle in practice, before in many places we
were forced to pre-computed the FQN eagerly (by calling
FQN.make_global), which defeated the whole idea.

Instead, we officialize the fact that we can precompute FQNs, and then
the VM emits an error if you end up with a duplicate.

The only place in which QNs were actually turned into multiple FQNs (by
appending a suffix) was for `W_AstFunc` closures, so we do it in an
ad-hoc way now.

Make it possible to create new types inside closures (#93)

This PR makes it possible to write code like this:
```
@h16477688c0e00699
def make_Point(T):
    class Point(struct):
        x: T
        y: T
    return Point
```

To do so, we had to teach the TypeChecker about `ClassDef`, and to
refactor the way FQNs are computed for types.

In particular, we cannot compute the unique FQN lazily inside
`vm.make_const`, because at that point it's too late: the FQN might have
already been used e.g. to create the FQN of a pointer. The solution is
to assign an unique FQN as soon as a new type is created.

For symmetry, we do the same also for `FuncDef`s.

message:
Refactor builtins (#95)

This PR is big, but most of the diff is just "moving things around".
The long term goals are to reduce circular dependencies between modules
imports, and preprare the ground for killing `._w`.

Highlights:
- it is now possible to use `Annotated[W_Object, w_my_type]` for
`@builtin_func` signatures. This gives a cleaner implementation of
`W_Dynamic` and removes the need to lot of `@no_type_check` in generic
functions such as in `ptr.py`
- `vm.b` now contains an empty `B` registry, which is populated by
`objects.py`, `primitives.py`, etc. This removes a lot of circular
dependencies
- kill `W_Void._w_singleton` and similar singletons for bools,
notimplemented, etc.: they now live directly on `B`.
  - `W_Dynamic` has been moved to `primitive.py`
- the handling of `__spy_members__` is now done by `W_Type.__init__`,
instead of `@builtin_type`

subject: Automatic declare forward references to types (#101)
message:
Automatic declare forward references to types (#101)

This is a big departure from Python semantics, but it's required to
write types having fields which directly or indirectly reference
themselves. Moreover, it makes writing type-annotated code much easier.
TL;DR, we can now do this:
```
def foo(x: MyType) -> void:
    ...

class MyType:
    ...
```

i.e., use `MyType` *before* its definition has been executed.
This is done by introducing the concept of `ForwardRef`, which is a
special object which can `become()` a new object.

With these new tools, we could finally make
`test_struct_with_ptr_to_itself` working, as in:
```
        class Node(struct):
            val: i32
            next: ptr[Node]
```

subject: Simplify W_OpImpl, introduce W_FuncAdapter, sanitize calling convention (#104)
message:
Simplify W_OpImpl, introduce W_FuncAdapter, sanitize calling convention (#104)

W_OpImpl was super messy and complicated because it served two purposes
at once:
1. An high-level description of which functions to call to implement a
certain OP, e.g. `W_OpImpl(w_foo)` or `W_OpImpl(w_foo, [wop_x, wop_y])`
2. A low-level description of how to actually call it: this was the
messy part because `typecheck_opimpl` mutated the opimpl implace to add
converters and do a whole mess with `wop.i`, and then consumers needed
to check with `.is_valid()`.

The idea is to split concerns into two separate types:
1. W_OpImpl serves the same (1) purpose as before
2. The (2) is now served by `W_FuncAdapter`, which knows how to
map/convert input arguments into output arguments and to call w_func.

Hopefully, soon we will also be able to kill other hacks such as
`W_OpArg.i` and `is_direct_call`.

Moreover, we also sanitize calling conventions. Until now we used
vm.call everywhere, but this was suboptimal because e.g. in case of
W_OpImpl we already *knew* that typechecking was done, so it was not
necessary to do it again in vm.call.

Now we have three layers of calls:
- `W_Func.raw_call`, `vm._raw_call`: this is the primitive upon which
all the rest is done. No type checking, no blue caching
- `vm.fast_call`: no typecheking, but respects the bluecache: this is
e.g. how you call opimpls after the typechecking was successfull
- `vm.call`: this is the most generic one, it does typechecking and it
can be used on arbitrary objects that implements `op_CALL`.

subject: Kill the Typechecker and do eager evaluation of blue expressions (#106)
message:
Kill the Typechecker and do eager evaluation of blue expressions (#106)

This PR fixes the following snippet of code:
```python
@h16477688c0e00699
def foo():   # "-> dynamic" is implicit
    return 42

def main() -> void:
    x = foo()
    print(STATIC_TYPE(x))
```

We want STATIC_TYPE(x) to be `i32`, because it's fully known at compile
time.

Untile now, we had two very separate phases of execution:
  - typechecking, in which we compute the type of each expression
  - execution/redshifting, in which we execute

The problem of this approach is that the TypeChecker cannot see "into"
blue calls, (because they will be executed only later) and so it's
unable to eagerly determine the type of "dynamic" blue values.

Another notable example of this:
```python
    buf = gc_alloc(i32)(1)
```

Until now, the typechecker thought that the type of `buf` was `dynamic`,
but now we can statically determine that it's `ptr[i32]`.

This PR kills the Typechecker and fuses its functionality directly
inside the ASTFrame, so that we can do a continuous
"evaluate-blue/typecheck-red" cycle.
The short summary of how it's done is this:
1. `W_OpArg` is now wrapper over `w_value` which keeps track of its
color, static type, symbol, location, etc
2. `W_OpArg` can be "abstract" (and thus have color, static type, etc.
but no actual value
3. The ASTFrame manipulates W_OpArg, and uses the symbol/location info
to emit precise errors like the TypeChecker used to do
4. The DopplerFrame subclasses the ASTFrame to perform redshifting,
where all red variables are represented by abstract W_OpArg,

This lets us to get rid of MANY hacks and workarounds, and it's a big
step forward.

Kill the ugly W_DirectCall hack (#108)

The need for this hack was explained by this now-removed comment in
`W_Func.op_CALL`:
```python
        """
        This is a bit of a hack.

        The correct opimpl for a W_Func object is something which says "please
        just call it". Ideally, we would like to do something like that:

            w_func = wop_func.blue_unwrap()
            return W_OpImpl(w_func, ...)

        However, we cannot because at the current moment, wop_func doesn't
        carry around it's blue value: this is something which needs to be
        fixed in the typechecker, eventually.

        The workaround is to wrap the functype inside a special W_DirectCall
        object, which is special cased by ASTFrame.
        """
```

But after #106 now we DO know the blue `w_func` at `op_CALL` time, so we
can kill all the crap described there.

As a bonus point, we also put a `def_loc` attribute on every `W_Func`,
so that we can always report the "true" definition line of functions in
case of errors.

subject: Introduce @builtin_method and use it for spy_new (#111)
message:
Introduce @builtin_method and use it for spy_new (#111)

This PR introduces a new decorator `@builtin_method`, which can wrap
interp-level methods of `W_*` classes into applevel methods.

Moreover, we use the new functionality to mark all existing `w_spy_new`
functions as `@builtin_method`s. This allows to simplify a lot some of
the ugly code in object.py.

In particular, we no longer need to create a custom metaclass for every
`W_*` class: now we can move `op_CALL` into `W_Type`, and eagerly look
up the method `__new__` from the blue class in order to know what to
call to instantiate a class.

We still support automatically-generated metaclasses but only when it's
really needed, e.g. for classes implementing `op_meta_GETITEM` and
similar.

subject: Kill W_ForwardRef, introduce types declaration/definition (#118)
message:
Kill W_ForwardRef, introduce types declaration/definition (#118)

Kill `W_ForwardRef`.
The big problem of `W_ForwardRef` is that they could work reliably only
for module-level definitions (because the `.become` happened in
`vm.add_global`): this means that e.g. this code:

```
@hb24089bc764d6f2e
class MyClass:
    __ll__: i32
    def __new__(cls) -> MyClass:
        ...
```

worked well at module level, but crashed inside the function.

Instead, introduce a two-step type initialization mechanism: types can
be in "declared" state, and then transition into a "defined" state. In
the next PRs, we will use this new feature to fix the case above.

Among the other things, this plays well with the need of lazy
initialization of some core types: instead of using an ad-hoc "lazy
setup" mechanism, we can just use the standard declare/define split.

The scope analyzer always assumed that if a symbol is present in a

we tried to find a symbol in an outer scope where the name was used,
instead of the scope where the name is DEFINED.

subject: Introduce support for lazy vs eager errors (#141)
message:
Introduce support for lazy vs eager errors (#141)

This PR introduces the new `--error-mode` flag, which can have these
values:
- `eager`: StaticErrors emitted during redshifting immediately abort the
compilation
  - `lazy`: StaticErrors are turned into `raise`s
- `warn`: same as `lazy`, but also prints the detected errors to stdout

This is best explained via an example:
```
def foo(x: bool) -> void:
    if x:
        print(1 + 2)
    else:
        print(1 + "hello")
```

With eager errors, you get a `TypeError` during redshifting.
With lazy errors, redshifting produces the following:
```
def foo(x: bool) -> void:
    if x:
        print_i32(3)
    else:
        raise TypeError('cannot do `i32` + `str`') # /.../astframe.py:360
```

Other highlights of the PR:
  - `operator::panic` is now `operator::raise`
- the SPy backend turns `operator::raise` into a `raise` stmt in pretty
print mode
- `SPyError` is no longer the root of a hierarchy of exeptions: there is
only a `SPyError`, which is a thin wrapper around `W_Exception`: the
actual hierarchy of errors is at app-level.
- Introduce `W_StaticError`: static errors are the ones who can be
lazyfied. `W_TypeError` is a subclass of `W_StaticError`, but the user
can raise `W_StaticError` explicitly

subject: Improve error messages when calling operators (#143)
message:
Improve error messages when calling operators (#143)

An example is worth 1000 words.
Consider this:
```python
from operator import OpImpl

@hb24089bc764d6f2e
class MyInt:
    __ll__: i32

    @h16477688c0e00699
    def __GETITEM__(v_obj, v_i):
        # this is the mistake, getitem should take an extra arg
        def getitem(m: MyInt) -> i32:
            return m.__ll__ + i*2
        return OpImpl(getitem)

def main() -> void:
    m = MyInt.__lift__(4)
    m[10]
```

Before this PR, you would get this error, which doesn't give any
information about which line actually triggered this call:
```
❯ spy /tmp/t.spy 
TypeError: this function takes 1 argument but 2 arguments were supplied
   --> /tmp/t.spy:10:9
 10 |         def getitem(m: MyInt) -> i32:
    |         ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ function defined here
```

With this PR, you get extra info:
```
❯ spy /tmp/t.spy 
TypeError: this function takes 1 argument but 2 arguments were supplied
   --> /tmp/t.spy:10:9
 10 |         def getitem(m: MyInt) -> i32:
    |         ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ function defined here

   --> /tmp/t.spy:16:5
 16 |     m[10]
    |     ^^^^^ operator::GETITEM called here
```

There is a lot of room for improvement and refinement, but for now this
should be good enough.

subject: Introduce @blue.generic (#145)
message:
Introduce @blue.generic (#145)

`@blue.generic` functions are exactly like `@h16477688c0e00699`, but they are
"called" using square brackets instead of parenthesis.
This makes it possible to write things like this:
```
@blue.generic
def add(T):
    def impl(x:T, y: T) -> T:
        return x + y
    return impl

def main() -> void:
    print(add[i32](1, 2))
    print(add[str]('hello ', 'world'))
```

In addition, there are a couple of minor/related updates:
- `W_FuncType` no longer includes argument names, only the argument
types
- we have different FQNs for red/blue/blue_generic functions, and we
simplified how to generate human-readable versions of them
  - improved Loc.get_src to work also in multiline case

subject: Add support for compiling multiple files (#158)
message:
Add support for compiling multiple files (#158)

The ultimate goal of this PR is to be able to import a `.spy` file from
another.
This is the list of changes to achieve that goal:
1. add `spy --imports` and `spy/analyze/importing.py` to statically
determine the set of modules needed to execute/compile a given spy entry
point

2. move scope.py and symtable.py into the new `spy/analyze` package

3. simplify and redesign the "toolchain" concept. Now we have a `target`
attribute, and a build system which is able to build for `native` (now
the default), `wasi` and `emscripten`.

4. kill `cbuild.py`: now the C compiler is no longer invoked directly:
instead, we use `ninja` to support compilation of multiple .c files;
`build/ninja.py` is responsible to both generate `build.ninja` and
execute it.

5. refactor the C backend: instead of producing a single .c file for a
given module, now we have a `CBackend` class which is responsible to
orchestrate multiple `CModWriter` instances, one for each `.c` file we
want to generate (and each `CModWriter` creates many `CFuncWriter`, one
per function")

Make it possible to use `raise WIP(...)` instead of doing `assert

error message instead of a compiler crash.
Moreover, we automatically add relevant location info to point to the
actual source code location which triggered the WIP.

For example:
```

    print(2 ** 3)

```
❯ spy /tmp/x.spy 
WIP: Operator not implemented yet: **
   --> /tmp/x.spy:2:11
  2 |     print(2 ** 3)
    |           |____| called from here
```

subject: make it possible to use None in function signatures (#189)
message:
make it possible to use None in function signatures (#189)

With this PR, we allow to do things like `def main() -> None`.

It is a bit involved, because:
1. `None` is not a type
2. functions `-> None` are expected to `return None`

We *could* probably solve it by creating a special object whose type is
itself (i.e. `type(None) is None`), but this would complicate the
typesystem unnecessarily.

Instead, we solve the problem by special casing `None` inside function
signatures: whenever we see `None`, we treat it as `NoneType`.
And then we apply the special case a bit here and there, mostly for
aesthetic reasons (e.g., when rendering function signatures we emit `->
None` instead of `-> NoneType`.
 
Moreover, we rename the old `W_Void` into `W_NoneType`, to be consisten
with Python.

subject: Introduce metafunctions (#192)
message:
Introduce metafunctions (#192)

This PR introduces the concept of metafunctions and the `@blue.metafunc`
decorator.

Metafunctions are a generalization of the two-phase dispatch concept
which is already in place for operators.
Calling a metafunc happens in two step:
1. blue call to the metafunc itself, passing `OpArg` as arguments, and
returning and `OpImpl`
2. red call to the returned `OpImpl`

This makes it possible to e.g. implement overloading, and to use it to
implement generic functions like `len()` and `print()`.

subject: Split OpSpec and OpImpl (#199)
message:
Split OpSpec and OpImpl (#199)

This is a no-op renaming of things.
Before:
  - OPERATORs returned W_OpImpl
  - typecheck() turned a W_OpImpl into a W_FuncAdapter
  - *however*, the return type of typecheck() was W_Func
- astframe and doppler had to pretend to deal with arbitrary W_Funcs
when calling their w_opimpl, thus adding complexity and indirection.

This PR creates two distinct concepts:
- `OpSpec`: the old OpImpl: it's what the user returns, and it's a
"high-level, non-typechecked" description of how to implement an op.
Usually, "call this func with these args"
- `OpImpl` is the old W_FuncAdapter, to underline that it's the concrete
way to execute an op
- OpImpl are executed by calling w_opimpl.execute() as opposed to
vm.fast_call(w_adapter) as it was before

message:
Better error messages when mistakenly importing .py files (#208)

Fixes #173 

Introduces new ImportError messages if you mistakenly try to import a
`.py` file. Example:
```
ImportError: cannot import `foo`
   --> /Users/anton/code/spy/examples/multifile/main.spy:3:1
  3 | import foo
    | |________| file `foo.py` exists, but py files cannot be imported

```

The two main bits of code needed to produce this error are in the method
`get_filename`, currently a member of `ImportAnalizyer`, and
`declare_Import` in `ScopeAnalyzer`. The main difficulty was to make the
logic in `get_filename` available while running `declare_Import`. I
implemented this by moving the `get_filename` method out of
`ImportAnalizyer` and into `SPyVM`, and adding a `check_py` flag to it
to detect matching `.py` files. This function already had a comment in
it, suggesting an alternate implementation:
```
    # XXX maybe THIS is the right place where to raise SPyImportError?
```
I looked into this briefly, but decided it would be a bigger refactor to
handle catching this error rather than moving `get_filename` to `SPyVM`,
where we can use it in the `ScopeAnalyzer`. Hopefully this refactor is
acceptable.

Don't duplicate W_FuncTypes unecessarily (#212)

This is a relatively heavy change in how types compares:
- by default types have `__spy_storage_category__ = 'reference'`, which
is basically "compare by identity" as its in python

tuples

subject: Simplify and speedup BlueCache (#213)
message:
Simplify and speedup BlueCache (#213)

The main point of the PR is to simplify the functioning of `BlueCache`:
up to now, it worked like this:
  - for each blue call, we record the functions and the list of `w_arg`s
- at lookup, we do a linear search along all the records and compare
each `w_arg` by equality using `vm.universal_eq`

This is problematic for many reasons:
  - it's slow
- it contains ugly recursion: to do e.g. a `CALL`, we need to compare
the `W_OpArg`s which are in the bluecache, and to compare them we need
to do more calls, etc.
  - as a result, it adds tons of noisy call frames to the tracebacks
- and we need to special case `W_OpArg` in vm.universal_eq to be able to
bootstrap the recursion

The new solution is faster and simpler:
- each applevel W_* object can be converted into an interp-level "key"
which can be put in an interp-level dict
  - to compare `w_arg` we can just compare thier keys
  - the default key for reference types is just `self`
- there is a sanity check to require value types to implement their
`spy_key`

As a benchmark, running `examples/bluefunc.spy` in interp mode (which
computes the value of `pi` and thus is pretty slow) is now ~25% faster.

subject: Deduplicate builtin functions (#216)
message:
Deduplicate builtin functions (#216)

This PR changes the way `W_BuiltinFunction`s are registered in the VM.

In particular, we removed the possibility of creating "dandling"
`@builtin_func`. Now, they can be created:
1. as part of a ModuleRegistry with `@MOD.builtin_func`
2. as part of a type with `@builtin_method`
3. directly attached to the vm with `@vm.register_builtin_func`

(3) in particular means that we CANNOT create multiple builtin funcs
with the same FQN. However, there is a common patter in interp-level
metafunctions which does exactly that, so we added special logic to
detect "same fqn, same code objects, same closure" and treat them as

message:
Forbid blue calls with red arguments (#217)

This fixes #190.
This example:
```
@h16477688c0e00699
def blue_inc(x):

def main() -> None:
    x = 2

```

  7 |     print(blue_inc(x))

  2 | def blue_inc(x):

   --> /tmp/t.spy:7:11

    |           |_________| operator::CALL called here
```

The biggest change which was needed to achieve this goal was to remove
the "temporary hack" inside `vm.call_OP`, which forcibly turned blue
args in red args in order to avoid unnecessary duplication of blue
closures. See #218 for details.

subject: Don't use FQNs for modules (#223)
message:
Don't use FQNs for modules (#223)

This is a *big* refactoring of how spy modules are represented
internally, which touches logic everywhere. It fixes #224, which
contains details of _why_ it's a problem.

This is a summary of what changed:

- `W_Module` no longer use `vm.globals_w` as a backing store. Each
`W_Module` now has its down `_dict_w` to contain the state. That's
basically the goal of the PR, all the rest was needed to achieve this
goal.

- Introduce the concept of `ImportRef`: when we do `from aaa import
bbb`, we record that this always represent a reference to `aaa.bbb`
(which will be resolved lazily, not implemented yet)

- `Symbol.fqn` was used for module-level constants/variables and
`import`ed names. Now we have `Symbol.impref` which is used only for the
latter. Module-level lookups are NOT resolved at `ScopeAnalizer` time,
they are correctly resolved by ASTFrame and then redshifted away.

- Mutable module-level "variables" are now represented by a `W_Cell`.
Each cell gets an FQN, and the content of the cell is mutable. Lookup of
cells is redshifted away, getting/setting the content is a red
operation. The C backend renders cells into C global variables (with an
unique name, thanks to the FQN).

- Cells will allow to have "mutable variables defined in a blue
closure". Not implemented yet.

- To detect that, ScopeAnalizer keeps track of `varkind` (`var` or
`const`) and `storage` (`direct` or `cell`) of each `Symbol`.

- Introduce specialized AST nodes for different kind of name
looku[/assignmet (local, direct, cell). This way the "lookup logic" is
executed only once in the ASTFrame the first time the name is accessed,
and then the redshifter sees only the specialized nodes which are
simpler and easier to shift. In particular, this is needed to deal with
Cells.

- The C backend no longer translates a `W_Module` into a .c file. Now it
translated a `CModule` into a .c file. A CModule groups together all the
FQNs of a given namespace. Of course there is still a strong
relationship between .spy and .c file, but now it maps more to where
PBCs are *defined* as opposed as where they are referenced.

- while we are at it, fix `spy --redshift --execute`, which was
executing the code BEFORE redshifting.

Decorators must be `@h16477688c0e00699` functions, but otherwise they work very
similarly to Python.

To make debugging easier, the "original" function is named e.g.
`mod::foo#__bare__`, so that it's clear that it doesn't necessarily
correspond to `mod.foo`.

Moreover, in this PR we modify the class FQN in two ways:
1. make sure it's immutable, and fix a bug which mutated the original
FQN when calling `with_suffix`
2. change (again!) the type of `FQN.suffix` from int to str. This is
needed to make it possible to use the `__bare__` suffix.

subject: For loops, range and iterators (#232)
message:
For loops, range and iterators (#232)

This PR implements support for `for` loops in the parser, ScopeAnalyzer
and ASTFrame. For loops don't use the classical `__iter__` protocol as
in Python. Instead, they use a new protocol called `__fastiter__`, which
is stateless and thus easier to optimize for the compiler.

In ASTFrame, the `for` loop is desugared into the equivalent `while`:
thanks to this, DopplerFrame and the C backend mostly work out of the
box.

Moreover, this PR also introduces the `range` object, implemented in
pure spy in `stdlib/_range.spy`. Currently it is not automatically
available as a builtin because we don't have the machinery to import spy
code as part of builtins.

Enable LTO when compiling in release mode: this is necessary to ensure
that gcc is able to inline the methods of the `__fastiter__` protocol
and produce optimal code.

Fix a bug in structs: emit a proper error if you try to get a
non-existent field.

Make it possible to pass structs INTO wasm test functions: this makes it
much easier to write certain kind of tests, like `test__range.py`.

subject: Implement generic List[T] for stdlib (#233)
message:
Implement generic List[T] for stdlib (#233)

This PR has been entirely written by claude code, including commit
messages and PR description.
The fully transcript of my conversation with claude is here:

https://antocuni.eu/files/claude-code/spy/spy.2025-09-30%20-%20implement%20List.html

---

## Summary

Implements a comprehensive generic `List[T]` type for the SPy standard
library, providing a dynamic array with Python-like list operations.

## Features Implemented

### Core functionality
- `List[T]()` - Create empty list with initial capacity
- `append(item)` - Add items with automatic capacity growth (2x
strategy)
- `len(list)` - Get current length
- `list[i]` - Read element by index
- `list[i] = value` - Modify element by index
- Negative indexing support (`list[-1]` for last element)

### Mutations
- `pop()` - Remove and return last element
- `insert(i, item)` - Insert at position with element shifting
- `clear()` - Remove all elements
- `remove(value)` - Remove first occurrence by value

### Iteration
- `__fastiter__()` - Fast iteration protocol
- `for x in list:` - Full for-loop support via `list_iterator` struct

### List operations
- `extend(other)` - Append all elements from another list
- `copy()` - Create shallow copy with independent memory
- `+` operator - Concatenate lists into new list
- `*` operator - Repeat list elements n times

### Searching
- `index(value)` - Find index of first occurrence
- `count(value)` - Count occurrences

### Comparison
- `==` operator - Type-safe equality using `@blue.metafunc`

## Implementation Details

- Uses low-level `ptr[T]` for memory management
- Generic implementation via `@blue.generic`
- Struct-based with `ListData` containing length, capacity, and items
pointer
- `@hb24089bc764d6f2e` decorator for lifted type implementation
- No reliance on unsupported features (no `break`, no `or/and` boolean
ops)

## Test Coverage

- **165 tests** passing across all 3 backends (interp, doppler, C)
- Comprehensive edge case testing:
  - Empty lists
  - Single elements
  - Capacity growth beyond initial size
  - Negative indexing boundary conditions
  - Type-specific operations (int, f64)
  - Error cases (IndexError, ValueError)

## Example Usage

```spy
from _list import List

def example() -> str:
    lst = List[int]()
    lst.append(10)
    lst.append(20)
    lst.append(30)
    
    lst[1] = 99          # Modify by index
    lst.remove(10)       # Remove by value
    
    lst2 = lst.copy()    # Shallow copy
    lst3 = lst + lst2    # Concatenate
    
    result = ''
    for x in lst3:
        result = result + str(x) + ' '
    return result
```

## Files Changed

- `stdlib/_list.spy` - Complete List[T] implementation (239 lines)
- `spy/tests/stdlib/test__list.py` - Comprehensive test suite (878
lines)

subject: Fix \x C literal generation for clang (#263)
message:
Fix \x C literal generation for clang (#263)

Fixes #255 

The C backend will turn the string `'\nball'` into the C literal string
`"\x0aball"`. clang will parse the beginning escape into a two byte hex
string followed by `'ll'`, which is not what we want, we want a single
byte escape sequence to encode the newline.

The solution implemented here is to use C string concatenation to ensure
that a `\x` only escapes one hex byte. The algorithm used here is to add
`""` to the beginning and end of `\x` escapes, when needed.

subject: Make it possible to have blue local vars (#267)
message:
Make it possible to have blue local vars (#267)

This PR makes it possible to have "blue local variables" inside a red
function. Fixes #261. This is needed e.g. for cases like this:

```python
def foo():
    T = int
    lst = List[T]()
```

in main, all the local vars are automatically red, and so `List[T]`
fails because `T` is red.

The solution is to make it possible to have "blue locals", in the most
intuitive way possible. In particular, a local is blue if:
1. it is assigned only once inside a function body
2. upon creation, it gets a blue value

List of features which were needed to achieve this goal:
  - parser support for `const` and `var` in all vardef places
- ScopeAnalyzer logic to automatically determine which local vars are
`const` and which are `var`.
- remove `Symbol.color`: the color of a symbol cannot be determined
statically, because it depends on the color of the rvalue. Move the
color to `LocalVar`, which live in `ASTFrame.locals`
- keep track of *why* a certain symbol is `var` or `const` via
`varkind_origin`: this is essential to make sure to produce good error
messages
- `ast.VarDef` now also contains the rvalue field, instead of relying on
a separate `ast.Assign`

  - introspection of variables and tab completion

subject: Playground build fixes (#306)
message:
Playground build fixes (#306)

This PR fixes a few recently discovered issues with the playground.

- Fixes #300. I added `build` as a dependency. Antonio reported it
didn't work for him as only a dev dependency. I don't see any harm
adding it as a regular dependency, since SPy is a developer tool in
itself.
- Fixes #296. I included `stdlib/` in both `MANIFEST.in` (for source
distributions) and `pyproject.toml` for wheels. The solution I used was
to add a `stdlib/__init.py` to make stdlib a python package, which
allows setuptools to easily package it. I realize this is not ideal,
since `stdlib/` is not actually a Python package, so I added a `raise`
to warn anyone who tries to import it from Python. I think this solution
might be ok for now, while we use CPython to bootstrap SPy we're
dependent on its build tools to develop SPy, so we might have to conform
to its rules for the time being. Still, happy to hear other ideas for a
solution if this isn't suitable for us.
- Removed the autodetection and use of `uv` in `playground/Makefile`.
Now it will use your $PYTHON env var or just `python`. I added a warning
comment about `emcc` breaking if you set $PYTHON to an executable with
arguments.
- I fixed a regression from commit b0f2b55a which broke the playground
links to the renamed example file `myarray.spy`.
- To try to prevent playground example file name mismatches, I DRY'ed
the list of example files in `playground/main.py` by reading the
manifest in `pyscript.toml`

There's more to look at as part of the epic #297, so I'll look more at
other improvements other PRs in the near future.

Introduce __spy__.interp_list (#335)

This PR is preparatory to the the ultimate goal is to make the builtin
`list` type an alias for `stdlib/_list.spy`.

We currently have a `list` type which is implemented _only_ in the
interpreter, and it's backed by an interp-level Python `list[W_Object]`.
We cannot just remove it altogether, because we need it for
bootstrapping reasons: in particular, the `OpSpec` app-level constructor
takes an applevel `list[MetaArg]`, and we need to be able to use it
within `_list.spy`.

The solution is to rename the old `list` into `__spy__.interp_list`,
which is still used for bootstrapping.
The next PR will re-introduce a proper `list` as an alias to
`_list.spy`.

subject: Create _list.list when using a list literal (#337)
message:
Create _list.list when using a list literal (#337)

`_list.List` has been renamed into `_list.list`, and made available as
`builtins.list` via implicit imports.
The syntax `[1, 2, 3]` creates an instance of `_list.spy::list` and
initialize it with the right items.

The interaction between interp and doppler is harder than expected.
Ultimately, `[1, 2, 3]` is translated into (simplified):
```
list[i32]()._push(1)._push(2)._push(3)
```

The problem is that we don't know that is the itemtype before evaluating
all the items, so we cannot do a simple AST transform as we do e.g. with
`for` loops. The solution is to implement the same logic twice:
1. in `ASTFrame`, we evaluate all the items, infer the itemtype, and
manually call the list ctor and all the pushes
2. in doppler, we first do abstract eval of (1) to infer the item type,
then discard the result and only then create the transformed AST.

Empty lists (`[]`) are still not supported, and for now you need to
instantiate the list explicitly, e.g. by doing `list[i32]()`.

Other misc changes:

- The former `list` object has been renamed to `__spy__.interp_list`,
and it's still needed for bootstrapping. In particular, `list[MetaArg]`
is implemented as `interp_list[MetaArg]`, because `list[MetaArg]` is
needed to compile `_list.spy`.
  - fix implicit imports in presence of .spyc files
  - `dir()` now returns `interp_list[str]` instead of `list[str]`
- improve the testing infrastructure so that now we can return nested
structs and structs with ptr fields by value
- add a workaround for a nasty MetaArg quicrk, see the comment in
`test_list_MetaArg_identity`

subject: refactor CONVERT (#338)
message:
refactor CONVERT (#338)

This PR augment and fixes `__convert_from__` and `__convert_to__`.

Until now, the internal machinery used a custom dispatch mechanism which
seemed to use OpSpec, but then discarded the extra args in case of
non-simple OpSpecs, causing lots of confusion.

This PR aligns `operator.CONVERT` to all the other operators and now
conversion OpSpec are fully supported. Morever, we change the signature
so that `__convert_from__` and `__convert_to__` always receive BOTH the
"expected type" and the "got type": this is useful in case of generics,
else when we do `__convert_from__` we cannot know which type we want to
convert into.

subject: Add support for empty list literals "[]" (#339)
message:
Add support for empty list literals "[]" (#339)

Make it possible to write things like:
```python
def main() -> None:
    l: list[i32] = []
    l.append(1)
    l.append(2)
    for i in l:
        print(i)
```

This works by making `[]` a special immutable singleton
`__spy__.empty_list`, and adding conversion rules to convert it to
`list[T]`.

There is no type inference at this stage, so untyped empty lists cannot
be mutated.

  File "/home/antocuni/anaconda/spy/venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/wasmtime/_bindings.py", line 3006 in wasmtime_func_call

subject: Fix 'Illegal instruction' crash caused by early wasmtime Engine creation
message:
Fix 'Illegal instruction' crash caused by early wasmtime Engine creation

wasmtime.Engine() installs signal handlers for WASM traps. When the Engine
is created at import time (module level), pytest's faulthandler.enable()
can overwrite these handlers, causing WASM traps to crash with "Illegal
instruction" instead of being properly caught as WasmTrap exceptions.

Fix by making ENGINE lazy (created on first use via get_engine()) instead
of at import time. This also makes the early-import sanity check in
conftest.py unnecessary, so remove it.

https://claude.ai/code/session_01UrpFDh8zgJL5uZJjKKYbSr

subject: Defer wasmtime Engine creation to avoid signal handler conflicts (#379)
message:
Defer wasmtime Engine creation to avoid signal handler conflicts (#379)

This replaces #378 with a different workaround.
It turns out that the problem originates from the fact that both pytest
and wasmtime try to install a `faulthandler`, and wasmtime should do it
later in order to "win".

The most proper fix is make the instantiation of `wt.Engine` lazy.

The following is the description generated by claude.

---


## Summary
Changed wasmtime Engine initialization from import-time to lazy
initialization to prevent signal handler conflicts with pytest's
faulthandler.

## Changes
- Replaced module-level `ENGINE = wt.Engine()` with a lazy-initialized
`_ENGINE` global variable
- Added `get_engine()` function that creates the Engine on first use
- Updated all Engine references in `LLWasmModule.__init__()` and
`LLWasmInstance.__init__()` to use `get_engine()`

## Details
The wasmtime Engine installs signal handlers for WebAssembly trap
handling at creation time. When the Engine was created at import time,
pytest's `faulthandler.enable()` could overwrite these handlers during
test initialization, causing WASM traps to crash with "Illegal
instruction" errors instead of being properly caught.

By deferring Engine creation until first use (typically during test
execution), the signal handlers are installed after pytest's
faulthandler setup, ensuring proper trap handling throughout test
execution.

subject: Implement tuple in the stdlib (#402)
message:
Implement tuple in the stdlib (#402)

Introduce `stdlib/_tuple.spy`, which implements `tuple` in SPy and thus
it's automatically supported by the C backend.

Tuples are implemented as structs like this:
```
struct tuple_int_int {
    int _item0;
    int _item1;
};
```

Moreover, the "tuple packing" syntax now automatically infers the right
tuple type and creates an instance of it: `STATIC_TYPE((1, 'hello')) ==
tuple[int, str]`.

Similarly, we support tuple unpacking: `a, b = sometuple`.

The old "blue only, untyped tuple" now lives in `__spy__.interp_tuple`.
It's still used for `*varargs`.

Unrelated misc changes:
- build `libspy.wasm` in a way that always include/exports all the
symbols which might be needed in tests

subject: Fix out-of-bounds src_colors in HTML AST visualizer
message:
Fix out-of-bounds src_colors in HTML AST visualizer

_get_src_colors walked all descendants and computed highlight positions
relative to the node's loc, but the actual src text (from _get_src) could
be shorter than the full descendant tree. This caused SVG highlight rects
to be drawn far outside their node's outline, appearing as spurious
blue/red blocks.

subject: Fix out-of-bounds src_colors in HTML AST visualizer
message:
Fix out-of-bounds src_colors in HTML AST visualizer

_get_src_colors walked all descendants and computed highlight positions
relative to the node's loc, but the actual src text (from _get_src) could
be shorter than the full descendant tree. For example, a ClassDef node's
src is just "class Foo:" (1 line) but its methods' colored expressions
span many more lines. This caused SVG highlight rects to be drawn far
outside their node's outline, appearing as spurious blue/red blocks.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 4.6 <noreply@anthropic.com>

subject: Encode src_colors as compact run-length string and fix multi-line dedenting
message:
Encode src_colors as compact run-length string and fix multi-line dedenting

Replace the list-of-dicts src_colors format with a compact run-length
string like "_9 B5 R3 _10" (blank/red/blue char counts). This resolves
overlapping color regions by building a flat per-character color map
(last/innermost write wins) before encoding.

Also fixes multi-line node src not being dedented: _get_src now calls
textwrap.dedent so nested nodes like For loops show unindented source.

The shared build_char_color_map/encode_color_map utilities in util.py
are also reused by colorize_sourcecode for terminal ANSI output.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 4.6 <noreply@anthropic.com>

This PR adds various improvements to the AST visualizer.

It adds a context menu to:

  - interactively hide/show leaves
  - make it possible to save a static svg version of a subtree

Moreover, it modifies `doppler.py` to keep also track of colors also
**shifted** expressions. This makes it possible to visualize colored
nodes also in `spy redshift`.
